full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the Vendors is directed against a judgment of affirmance in a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 The co-sharer, filed an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act claiming to be a co-sharer in the holding to pre-empt a transfer made by the vendors in favour of the pre-emptee on 4.2.66. 

 4. Mr. Maksudur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the Vendors, contended that the right of preemption is subject to the reconveyance and in support of the proposition, referred to the case of Sital Chandra Koley and another Vs. Mihilal Koley and ors. 58 C.W.N. 1000 and the case of Basanta Kumar Churnakar Vs. Durganath Pal and others 43 C.W.N. 549 and the case of Biswawar Roy Vs. Joytennessa and others 13 D.L.R. .287. He further referred to the case of Abul Hossain (minor) and others Vs. Md. Masim Ali and others 19 D.L.R. 677. Referring to these decisions Mr. Moksudur Rahman submits that, the decree passed in Title Suit No. 116 of 1966 is good and the learned Courts below had no jurisdiction to term the same as collusive and fraudulent on no evidence. The said decree, according to the learned Advocate is a valid and binding decree as between the parties to the suit and unless the same is set aside, the courts below had no jurisdiction to term the same as fraudulent and collusive and so grant pre-emption overlooking the effect of the said decree. The property in suit was sold on 4.2.66 and on the same date the contract for reconveyance took place by an unregistered agreement. The pre-emptor filed the application for pre-emption on 2.6.66 Title Suit No. 116 of 1966 was filed for specific performance of the contract against the present pre-emptee and the suit was decreed an expert on 9. 66. The instant application for pre-emption was allowed by the learned Munsif on: 24.4.67. It, therefore, appears that before the pre-emption was allowed the pre-emptee lost his title to the land by virtue of the decree. Mr. Maksudur Rahman has drawn my attention to the kabalas executed by Abdul Majid in favour of Yakub Khan and Madhu Khan by sale deed Nos. 3299 and 3298 respectively on 15-12.72. It is, therefore, evident that with the execution of the kabalas tears of the decree for specific performance of contract, nothing remained with the pre-emptee which could be preempted by the preemptor. The Vendors are admittedly co-sharers of the preemptor. Since the pre-emptor cannot have a better title than what the pre-emptee had it follows that the pre-emptor was bound; the contract for reconveyance. In terms of the contract, there was a decree and thereafter' the property was duly reconveyed as stated above. In the circumstances the right of pre-emption which accrued in favour of the pre-emptor on the transfer dated 4-2-66 no longer subsists in vim of the reconveyance already made by the pre-emptee in favour of the Vendors and accordingly the pre-emption appears to be in fructuous. The authorities referred to above hold good in the case where subsequent reconveyance did not take place. It is trite that the right of the pre-emptor is not defeated by a subsequent reconveyance but the same is in-effective against the original co-sharers in whose favour the property reverted lawfully. In the circumstances the contention of Mr. Moksudur Rahman is not without substance. 

 5. Mr. Abu Taher Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party contends that the learned Courts below concurrently found that the agreement for reconveyance and the exparte decree obtained in the Title Suit No. 116 of 1966 are collusive and fraudulent and the same did not affect the right of pre-emption. As observed already, the right of pre-emption accrued lawfully in favour of the pre-emptor but the same ceased of be operative against the original co-sharers due to the reconveyance. Mr. Abu Taher Chowdhury could not refer to any authority, to justify the finding of the learned Courts below that the agreement for reconveyance and the decree could be nullified in a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It has already been observed that the parties to Title Suit No. 116 of 1966 are bound by the decree and unless the same is set aside in an appropriate proceeding, the effect thereof cannot be brushed aside by observing that the same was collusive and fraudulent. In the circumstances the contention of Mr. Chowdhury does not appear to explain coherently the circumstance appearing in the instant case. 

 For the reasons stated above the Rule is made absolute without costs. The judgment and order of the courts below are set aside and the application for pre-emption is rejected.
